title: Fair Feedback, Retention, and Transitions
before: A conversation about feedback that names the work and its conditions, and about keeping support in place through transitions.

turns.text: This course is Fair Feedback, Retention, and Transitions. It’s mostly for supervisors, though anyone who gives feedback or has growth conversations will find it useful. The focus is on feedback that’s specific about the work and the conditions around it, instead of personality or identity. That kind of feedback becomes the foundation for fair retention and smoother transitions.

The opening example is a piece of practice feedback: be more professional. What action does it point to? What expectation, or what effect? The course asks us to turn that impression into a question about the work. A concern can stay serious while becoming specific enough for the person to understand and actually address.

The key distinction is between observation, effect, and inference. An observation describes what occurred. An effect is what the event changed or made harder. An inference proposes an explanation. So a delayed response is an event, while lack of commitment is a much broader judgment, and it may not follow without more evidence.

The first practice situation applies that to services. A review calls a provider uncommitted after delayed responses, but nobody has looked at changed instructions or a handoff. You’ll decide what should happen. The course notes that repeated character judgments can hide a process barrier and shape how someone is treated later, which makes this more than a wording choice.

Feedback also depends on expectations being clear before evaluation, so a later review shouldn’t introduce a hidden criterion. Evidence should cover the whole period and the actual responsibilities. A recent mistake or a visible presentation can dominate memory, while coordination and support work go unnoticed simply because they’re less memorable. That’s a quiet way people’s contributions disappear.

I’d add the point about warmth. The course says warmth doesn’t require vague praise or avoiding a concern. Clear, respectful feedback can name a difficult issue and still preserve the person’s dignity. The person also deserves a chance to respond through the actual process. Disagreement isn’t disloyalty, though a response doesn’t automatically erase the concern either.

The second practice situation is about a review that credits an employee’s presentations but leaves out substantial coordination work and development tasks the employee couldn’t access. You’ll choose the useful response. The course is careful that a pattern like this may affect later development and retention, while its cause still needs evidence.

On retention, the course suggests asking relevant questions with a clear purpose and appropriate privacy, before and after a departure. One account doesn’t explain every departure, and a missing response doesn’t mean satisfaction. When a conversation raises harassment, discrimination, accommodation, or safety, informal feedback isn’t the route. Those matters go to the responsible office, and you respond within your role.

Transitions get their own attention. The third situation describes a new supervisor removing a work arrangement that helped an employee participate, then describing the resulting difficulty as poor adaptation. You’ll decide what should be examined. The course is clear that private details aren’t general transition material, and that a course can’t approve an accommodation.

Near the end, you’ll privately rewrite a practice statement: the provider does not care because responses are late. The task is to name the event, the expectation, the possible effect, and the missing context. You keep the concern serious while making the next inquiry specific enough to actually examine.

As you go, think of a piece of feedback you’ve given or received recently. Did it name something the person could see and act on? Was any part of the work left out? Bring that example with you. Supportive practice is clear about concerns, honest about unknowns, and respectful of both the person and the process.

guidance.title: Separating the three
guidance.text: Before you write feedback, try listing what happened, what it affected, and what you think explains it, on separate lines. The third line is often where judgments about character slip in. Keep the first two firm and hold the third loosely. Ask the person what they saw. Their account may confirm your explanation, change it, or reveal a condition you didn’t know about.

guidance.title: What carries forward
guidance.text: Think about someone whose role, supervisor, or assignment changed recently, perhaps your own. Which expectations stayed clear, and which support carried over? Was any recurring work left out of how their contribution was described? Consider one question you could ask, at the next review or handoff, that would help the person’s work and conditions stay visible.
